blocks.text: Daniel spread the newspaper across his workbench and held its corners down with a screwdriver and an empty cup. Super Zerdo looked back at him from a street photograph, the tank cradled against his blue suit.
Luke hovered beside the lamp. “What are you looking at him for?”
Daniel laid his experiment notes beside the photograph. “Because power isn’t the only thing we need.”
“I thought that was what Skyfall was for.”
“It is. The fireball supplies the energy. But to put you back into a body, I need one that can survive the procedure.”
Luke looked toward the old cot beneath the shelves. He remembered lying there with a broken jaw, trusting his uncle to make it right.
“Can’t you use mine?”
Daniel’s pencil stopped. “We have to work with what’s available.”
“That isn’t an answer.”
Daniel turned a page in his notes. Luke drifted after it, unwilling to let him change the subject again.

“A normal human body wouldn’t withstand the energy,” Daniel said. “Zerdo pulled steel apart. He jumped off that robot carrying a tank and landed on his feet. Whatever changed him made him stronger than ordinary flesh should be.”
He tapped the photograph.
blocks.alt: In Daniel’s cluttered laboratory, Daniel points to Super Zerdo’s photograph in an old newspaper beside his experiment notes. Luke’s floating blond head and iron jaws hover over the bench, his expression tempted but uneasy.

blocks.text: “He’s the only one I’ve found who could survive it.”
Luke studied the boy’s red mask. “You mean make me strong like him?”
“I mean use his body.”
For a moment, the ticking meter on the bench was the loudest thing in the room.
Luke moved nearer the newspaper. “His actual body?”
“Arms. Legs. All that strength.” Daniel pushed the notes toward him. “And your mighty iron jaws.”

Luke looked down at the photograph, imagining hands beneath his chin. He could lift the bench. He could walk out of the laboratory instead of drifting through a window. If the glove came at him again, he would have something to hit it with.
“With your jaws and Zerdo’s super body,” Daniel said, “you’d be unstoppable.”
Luke’s eyes lifted. “I could bend steel with my hands.”
“And bite through it.”
The thought pleased him more than he wanted his uncle to see. Daniel saw it anyway. He pulled up a stool and began sketching beside the photograph.

Then Luke remembered the boy holding up the café roof. He had barely managed to get past the glove that day. Zerdo had torn a giant robot apart since then. Luke had told his uncle he wasn’t fighting them again. Somehow, Daniel had made another attack sound like a way out.
“It won’t be easy,” he said.
“Of course. A procedure like this takes preparation.”
“I mean getting him here.” Luke looked directly at his uncle. “He stopped your robot. I can’t just pick him up and carry him through the door.”
Daniel glanced toward the rear workshop. A thick cable lay across the floor beside the collector’s unfinished frame.
“He won’t be doing any lifting while I work.”
“You still have to catch him.”
“I know.”
Luke returned his gaze to the photograph. Near Zerdo, an indistinct pink figure stood beside the rescued tank. Even with the newspaper folded beneath the cup, he could see how close they were.
“What happens to him?”
Daniel’s pencil paused above the sketch.
“When you’ve given me his body,” Luke said. “What happens to Zerdo?”
“We’re a long way from that.”
“You just said—”
“And we’ll get nowhere if you argue about every step before I’ve finished planning it.” Daniel laid the pencil down. “I thought you wanted me to put you right.”
Luke turned away. He did want it. He wanted to pull on a shirt, tie his shoes, reach for a doorknob. He also wanted to know why his uncle would not answer the question.
Behind him, Daniel shifted the cup off the newspaper. The rest of Jenny’s article unfolded beneath it.
“He won’t come here willingly,” Luke said.
Daniel looked from the photograph to the reporter’s name beneath the headline. He picked up his pencil again.
“Then we’ll give him a reason.”
